title: When Great Trees Fall
author: Maya Angelou
tagline: Poem · elegy · grief at the death of great people and the peace of remembering them

overview.intro: The poem compares the death of great people to the falling of great trees. When a huge tree comes down in a forest, the whole natural world reacts: powerful animals feel fear and small creatures fall silent. In the same way, when a great soul dies, human beings feel the shock. The world seems thinner and emptier, and people are filled with grief and with a painful awareness of what they did not say. But the poem does not end in despair. Slowly, a quiet peace arrives, and the memory of the departed becomes a source of strength and inspiration to live better.

learn.title: What the poem says, stage by stage

blocks.text: This is a broad paraphrase in our own words. Read the poem in your textbook and match each stage to the lines.

items: Stage 1 (nature is shaken): when a great tree falls, the effect spreads far beyond the spot. Even hard, distant parts of the landscape and powerful creatures feel the disturbance and are afraid.
Stage 2 (small things fall silent): in the forest the smaller living things draw back into silence. Their fear is so deep that their senses seem worn away.
Stage 3 (the human loss): when a great soul dies, the air around us feels thin and empty. For a short while we see everything with a painful clearness.
Stage 4 (memory and regret): our memory sharpens and returns to kind words we meant to say but did not. We regret what was left undone.

Stage 5 (the world shrinks): because our own lives were shaped by these great people, their going leaves us diminished and confused. We feel like people left in a cold, dark place, unable to think clearly.

Stage 6 (peace and inspiration): then, slowly and faintly, a quiet comes. We realise that they lived, and that this fact remains. Their example gives us a peace that will not go away, and the strength to live better lives because they once existed.

blocks.text: The death of a great person is a shattering loss, felt by everything around them, but their life leaves a lasting gift. Grief passes into peace when we remember what they were and let their example guide us. The poem moves from the shock of loss to the consolation of legacy.

items: Opening: solemn and heavy, with a mood of fear and shock as the natural world reacts.
Middle: sorrowful and regretful, as memory turns to what was left unsaid.
Close: calm, consoling and quietly hopeful. The mood lifts as peace and inspiration replace despair.
The change in tone follows the change in feeling: grief first, acceptance later.

items.meaning: Great people are compared to great trees throughout the first part of the poem. Like a tall tree, a great person gives shelter, presence and stability, and their fall leaves a gap that everything nearby feels.
Pictures of fear in the natural world and of a thin, empty atmosphere let the reader feel the physical effect of grief.
Mighty creatures and tiny ones react in different ways, and grief at the start of the poem contrasts with peace at the end. The contrast shows how deep the loss is and how much healing can follow.
Nature is shown reacting with fear and silence like a grieving person, and the tree stands for a noble, strong life that shelters others.
The absence of a strict rhyme scheme lets the lines rise and fall like natural speech and feeling. The slow, steady movement suits a poem of mourning.
The poem sets the fall of trees beside the death of great souls, so the second part echoes the first and the comparison is clear.

items: Always mention the two halves of the poem: the shock of loss and the arrival of peace.
When explaining the metaphor, say what a great tree is like (tall, strong, sheltering) and link this to great people.
Remember that the ending is hopeful. A poem about death that ends in peace and inspiration should not be described as only sad.
Refer to the poem's lines in your own words; you do not need exact quotation to earn marks for understanding.

keyPoints: The poem compares the death of great people to the fall of great trees.
When a great tree falls, powerful creatures feel fear and small things fall silent.
When a great soul dies, humans feel emptiness, sharper memory and regret for words left unsaid.
The loss makes us feel diminished, because our lives were shaped by those who have gone.
Slowly, peace comes, along with a lasting inspiration to live better because they existed.
examFocus: Explain the central comparison between trees and great souls.
How does nature react to the fall of a great tree?
Describe the feelings of people who lose a great person.
How does the poem move from grief to consolation?
The tone and mood of the poem, and how they change.
Devices: extended metaphor, imagery, contrast, free verse.

questions.prompt: What does the fall of a great tree stand for in the poem?
options: The cutting down of forests by humans
The death of a great person
questions.answer: The death of a great person.
questions.explanation: The poem sets the fall of great trees beside the death of great souls, so the tree is a metaphor for a noble, strong life.
questions.commonMistake: Reading the poem as a description of nature alone.

questions.prompt: How do the small creatures of the forest respond when a great tree falls?
options: They fall into a fearful silence
They rush to feed on the fallen tree
questions.answer: They fall into a fearful silence.
questions.explanation: The poem uses silence to show that the fear is deeper than any noise or movement.
questions.commonMistake: Assuming that fear must be shown by noise.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the movement of the poem as a whole?
options: From fear and grief to peace and inspiration
questions.answer: From fear and grief to peace and inspiration.
questions.explanation: The poem opens with shock and loss, moves through regret, and ends with lasting peace and the encouragement to live well.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the poem ends in sorrow. The final part is consoling.

questions.prompt: How does the natural world react when a great tree falls, according to the poem?
questions.answer: The disturbance spreads widely. Powerful creatures and even the hard features of the landscape feel the shock and are afraid, and the smaller living things go into a fearful silence. The whole natural world feels the loss, not only the place where the tree stood.
questions.explanation: Two marks: fear among the large and powerful, silence among the small.
questions.commonMistake: Saying nature does not notice the fall.

questions.prompt: What feelings does the poet say people experience when a great soul dies?
questions.answer: People feel that the world around them has become thin and empty. For a while they see everything with a painful clarity. Their memory grows sharper and turns to the kind words they never spoke, so they feel regret. Because their own lives were shaped by the departed, they also feel smaller and lost, as though left in a cold, dark place.
questions.explanation: Include the emptiness, the regret and the sense of being diminished.
questions.commonMistake: Mentioning only sadness without the regret and the sense of being lost.

questions.prompt: Explain how the comparison between trees and great souls works in the poem. Why is a tree a good image for a great person?
questions.answer: A great tree is tall, strong and long-lived, and it gives shelter, shade and stability to the creatures around it. A great person does the same for those who depend on them, giving guidance, protection and inspiration. When the tree falls, everything nearby feels the loss, and when a great person dies, family, friends and even the wider world are shaken. The extended metaphor lets the poet describe human grief through the reactions of nature, so the reader can feel its size and its effect on many lives.
questions.explanation: Explain what a tree is like, link each quality to a great person, and show how the comparison is developed.
questions.commonMistake: Stating the comparison without explaining why the image suits great people.

questions.prompt: The poem is about grief, but it does not end in despair. Discuss how the poet moves from loss to consolation.
questions.answer: The first part of the poem dwells on shock: the natural world trembles, small creatures fall silent, and human beings feel an empty, thin world and a bitter clearness of vision. The middle deals with regret, as memory returns to what was not said, and the sense of being reduced and lost without the guiding presence of the departed. The final part changes the direction. Slowly, and faintly at first, a peace arrives, and the poet says that what remains is the fact that these people lived. Their example becomes a source of strength and pushes those left behind to live better. The tone changes from heavy and solemn to calm and hopeful, and the structure of the poem, moving from fall to legacy, itself carries the message that grief, though real, is followed by renewal.
questions.explanation: Follow the three movements (shock, regret, peace), refer to the change in tone, and end with the message.
questions.commonMistake: Describing only the sad first half of the poem.

questions.prompt: What is the final message that the poem leaves the reader about those who have died?
questions.answer: The poem says that the great do not disappear without a trace. Their existence itself is a lasting gift, and the memory of what they were brings peace to those who remain. It also inspires the living to try to live better lives, so the departed continue to influence the world even after their death.
questions.explanation: Mention peace, memory and inspiration to live better.
questions.commonMistake: Giving only the idea of sorrow at the loss.

questions.prompt: Think of a person in your own life or in public life whose influence remains after they are gone. How does the poem help you understand the effect of their loss and their legacy?
questions.answer: I think of a grandparent, or of a teacher or public figure who shaped many lives, and the poem helps me see two things. First, the loss is bigger than a single family's sadness, just as a great tree falling affects the whole forest: many people feel less secure and less guided. Second, the poem points out that regret for unspoken kindness is common, which encourages me to express appreciation while people are still with us. It also shows how the memory of such a person can become a source of calm and strength, since their values continue in those they taught. The poem therefore helps me see mourning as a stage that leads towards gratitude and a wish to live up to their example.
questions.explanation: Any suitable person may be chosen. Link the personal example clearly to ideas in the poem, such as wide loss, regret and legacy.
questions.commonMistake: Writing about the person in detail and forgetting to use the poem.

questions.prompt: Why is free verse a suitable form for a poem about grief and remembrance?
questions.answer: Free verse has no fixed rhyme scheme or line pattern, so the lines can follow the natural rise and fall of speech and emotion. This suits grief, which does not follow neat patterns, and it lets the poet move slowly from shock to peace without forcing the feeling into a set shape. The unforced rhythm keeps the tone sincere and solemn.
questions.explanation: Say what free verse is, then link its freedom to the subject and the mood.
questions.commonMistake: Defining free verse without connecting it to the poem's theme.
